1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 1,312 kWh (29,918 − 28,606), line items sum to $238.89 ($18.79 + $45.62 + $174.48), and the change versus last month is +$31.53 ($238.89 − $207.36); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map both billing periods to the AEP Ohio tariff by date: last month (2026-07-30 to 2026-08-27) and current (2026-08-27 to 2026-09-30) both fall entirely under the post-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.788; tier-1 variable $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh for the first 2,000 kWh), so there is no rate change and price_usd = 0.

3. Compute days_usd from the longer period: 34 days versus 28 days (+6 days); value the extra days at last month's average daily bill ($207.36 ÷ 28 ≈ $7.41/day), giving roughly +$44.43, or consistently assign length-related consumption to usage instead.

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 263.5 / HDD 0) to current (CDD 270 / HDD 38), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective variable rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly +$31.53; this captures household usage changes not explained by price, days, or weather.

6. Check for a billing error: model the current period with the tariff (fixed $18.788 + 1,312 kWh × $0.1677638 ≈ $238.89) and compare to the actual $238.89; both match within rounding, so billing_error_suspected = false and billing_error_usd = null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
